Also, like the surface temperature has some effect in absorbing the heat or something, no?

The surface composition absorbing solar radiation has an effect on heat retention and release over time (aka the urban heat island effect). This comes about primarily from the emissivity and reflectance of a surface. Highly emissive surfaces (asphalt pavement) freely absorb and emit thermal radiation, while highly reflective surfaces (mirrors) do not absorb heat as they literally reflect it away. So the variance in surface material over any given patch of land, can be quantitatively analyzed for heat absorption, emittance, and retention. Ultimately this results in urban centers being statistically warmer than suburban or non-urban areas (grassland, forest, etc.).

Water is actually quite reflective, but has it's own intricacies, particularly since as a medium, light has trouble propagating through it. This results in water being very cool with depth, as solar radiation simply cannot impart a significant amount of heat transfer to the medium to significantly increase it's overall temperature, thanks to it's reflectiveness. This of course goes back to the whole angle of incidence stuff I previously mentioned and can be complex too with waves and non-laminar behavior.

When examining thermodynamic systems, we primarily concern ourselves with energy input to the system. Since energy has to be conserved, any energy input has to be equivalent to an energy output (Qin = Qout). I won't go into detail, but suffice it to say that for a system, we can have heat sources (where energy emanates from) and heat sinks (where energy flows to). Any cumulative effects, would be a system level definition or analysis.

In the case of the planet, oceans don't tend to function as solar heat sinks because they reflect radiation off, while organic and earthen components of the planet, readily absorb heat, and as such function as a sink (as heating of the ground only extend to a few inches below the surface, hence caves of certain depth are cold, sand and soil of a certain depth are cool).

Ultimately, defining all of that (heat island, reflectance, and sinks) will be a cumulative or system level effect, and system scope can vary between specific and general.
